title: TRI 2025 - Most Popular Sri Lankan Tea Cultivar
content: TRI 2025 is the most widely cultivated tea variety in Sri Lanka, developed by the Tea Research Institute. This Cambod-type cultivar originated from the ASM 4/10 clone and was released for commercial planting due to its exceptional adaptability. TRI 2025 demonstrates remarkable versatility, thriving in low country, mid country, and up country elevations. The cultivar exhibits strong resistance to blister blight disease caused by Exobasidium vexans and shows tolerance to root-lesion nematode (Pratylenchus loosi). Additionally, TRI 2025 possesses drought tolerance, making it suitable for regions with irregular rainfall patterns. The tea produced from this cultivar has a well-balanced flavor profile suitable for both orthodox and CTC processing methods.

title: Nuwara Eliya - The Champagne of Ceylon Tea
content: Nuwara Eliya, often called 'Little England', produces the most delicate and prized Ceylon teas. Located at an average elevation of 1,868 meters (6,128 feet), it represents the highest tea-growing region in Sri Lanka. The cool climate, with temperatures rarely exceeding 20°C, results in slow leaf growth that concentrates flavor compounds. Nuwara Eliya teas are characterized by their exceptionally light, golden liquor with greenish-yellow tones - the lightest of all Ceylon teas. The flavor profile features exquisite bouquet with delicate fragrance, brightness, and briskness. Distinctive notes of cypress, wild mint, and eucalyptus distinguish these teas. The Western Quality Season from January to March and Eastern Quality Season in August-September produce the finest teas when cool, dry winds enhance quality. Nuwara Eliya tea is often compared to Champagne in the wine world - representing the pinnacle of Ceylon tea excellence.

title: Uva - Unique Monsoon-Influenced Teas
content: Uva is a distinctive tea region producing some of the most exotic Ceylon teas due to its unique exposure to both the northeast and southwest monsoons. Located on the eastern slopes of the central highlands at 1,000-1,600 meters (3,000-5,000 feet), Uva experiences weather patterns unlike any other tea region. The famous Uva Season from July to September occurs when the Cachan wind - a dry wind from the northeast monsoon - sweeps across the region, causing leaves to dehydrate slightly on the bush. This natural withering concentrates flavor compounds, producing teas with distinctive mellow, smooth, and exotic aromatic character. The bright, coppery liquor and unique flavor profile have made Uva teas highly prized. Thomas Lipton famously introduced Americans to tea using Uva teas, establishing the region's international reputation. Uva teas are particularly valued in Middle Eastern and European markets.

title: Elevation Categories and Tea Quality
content: Sri Lankan tea is classified into three elevation categories that fundamentally influence tea character. High Grown (Up Country) teas from above 1,200 meters produce the most delicate, complex, and prized teas with light liquor and subtle flavors. Medium Grown (Mid Country) teas from 600-1,200 meters balance body and flavor, producing versatile teas with good strength and character. Low Grown (Low Country) teas from below 600 meters produce bold, strong teas ideal for blending and traditional preparations. The elevation effect relates to temperature - cooler temperatures slow leaf growth, allowing accumulation of flavor compounds, amino acids, and aromatic substances. Higher elevation teas command premium prices, while low elevation teas provide volume and strength for commercial blends. title: Orange Pekoe (OP) - Premier Whole Leaf Grade
content: Orange Pekoe (OP) is the highest main grade of whole leaf Ceylon tea, representing the standard for quality leaf tea production. Despite its name, Orange Pekoe contains no orange flavoring - the term likely derives from the Dutch House of Orange or the copper color of oxidized leaf. OP consists of long, wiry, thin leaves that are carefully rolled to preserve their integrity. The leaves unfurl beautifully when brewed, releasing delicate fragrance and producing a light to medium bodied infusion. OP teas are prized for their smooth character without bitterness when properly brewed. This grade is typically produced from the youngest leaves and represents careful plucking and processing standards. OP is the benchmark grade against which other whole leaf grades are compared.

title: Orthodox Tea Manufacturing Process
content: Orthodox processing is the traditional method of tea manufacture that Sri Lanka has made its specialty, accounting for 95% of the country's production. The process begins with plucking, ideally two leaves and a bud. Withering follows, lasting 12-20 hours to reduce moisture content by approximately 50%, making leaves pliable for rolling. Rolling is a critical step lasting 30-60 minutes that breaks cell walls, releases enzymes, and creates the characteristic twisted leaf shape. During oxidation (often incorrectly called fermentation), enzymes convert catechins to theaflavins and thearubigins over 2-4 hours under controlled temperature and humidity. Finally, drying halts oxidation and reduces moisture to approximately 3% for shelf stability. Orthodox processing produces complex, layered flavors with distinct regional character that distinguishes Ceylon tea in world markets.

title: Blister Blight - Most Severe Leaf Disease
content: Blister blight caused by Exobasidium vexans is the most economically important leaf disease of tea in Sri Lanka, particularly devastating in high-elevation regions. The disease appears as circular blister-like swellings on young leaves, initially pale green then developing white powdery spore masses on the undersurface. Severe infections cause leaf distortion, defoliation, and significant yield loss. Favorable conditions include cool temperatures (15-20°C), high humidity, and continuous wet weather - conditions common in up country regions during monsoon periods. Infected leaves produce poor quality tea with off-flavors. Management includes resistant cultivars (TRI 2025, TRI 3019, TRI 4006, TRI 5001-5004), copper fungicide applications, and cultural practices promoting air circulation. Climate-smart cultivar selection is increasingly important as weather patterns shift.

title: Root-Lesion Nematode in Tea
content: Root-lesion nematode (Pratylenchus loosi) is a significant pest affecting tea productivity throughout Sri Lanka. These microscopic worms attack tea roots, causing lesions that impair nutrient and water uptake. Above-ground symptoms include stunted growth, yellowing leaves, poor recovery after pruning, and progressive decline. Nematode damage is often mistaken for nutrient deficiency or drought stress. Heavily infested fields may lose 20-40% of potential yield. The pest is particularly problematic in replanting situations where new plants are established in infested soil. Management options include tolerant cultivars (TRI 2025, TRI 4052, TRI 4053, TRI 5003), soil fumigation before replanting, and organic matter applications that encourage nematode-suppressing soil organisms. Nematode-free planting material is essential for new establishments.

title: Shot Hole Borer Beetle
content: Shot hole borer (Euwallacea fornicatus) is an ambrosia beetle that attacks tea stems, causing significant damage in Sri Lankan plantations. The beetle bores small circular holes into woody stems to cultivate fungal gardens that feed their larvae. This damage weakens branches, disrupts nutrient flow, and can cause dieback of affected sections. Heavy infestations kill entire bushes. Stressed plants are more susceptible - drought, poor nutrition, and heavy plucking increase vulnerability. Signs include small entry holes, sawdust accumulation, wilting of affected branches, and fungal staining of wood. Management includes removing and destroying affected branches, maintaining plant vigor, and using resistant cultivars. TRI 5001 shows notable resistance to shot hole borer, while TRI 5002-5004 are susceptible. Chemical control is difficult as beetles live inside stems.

title: Red Spider Mite Damage
content: Red spider mite (Oligonychus coffeae) causes significant foliar damage in tea, particularly during dry periods. These tiny arachnids feed on leaf undersurfaces, puncturing cells and extracting contents. Damage appears as bronze or reddish discoloration of upper leaf surfaces, with fine webbing visible underneath. Severe infestations cause defoliation and reduced photosynthesis, impacting both yield and quality. Hot, dry conditions favor mite population explosions - outbreaks often follow drought periods. Natural enemies including predatory mites help control populations in balanced ecosystems. Chemical control is sometimes necessary but risks disrupting beneficial organisms. Cultural practices including shade management, irrigation during drought, and avoiding excessive nitrogen fertilization help prevent outbreaks. Mite-damaged leaves should be excluded from harvest as they produce poor quality tea.

title: Sri Lanka Tea Industry Statistics
content: Sri Lanka is the fourth largest tea producer globally and second largest exporter of orthodox tea. The industry encompasses approximately 188,000 hectares of tea cultivation, producing around 298,000 tonnes annually. Tea accounts for approximately 15% of agricultural GDP and provides direct employment to over 1 million people, with indirect employment reaching 2 million. Sri Lanka holds approximately 19% of world tea export market share. The industry includes both large estates (plantations over 10 hectares) and smallholders (under 10 hectares). Smallholders now contribute over 75% of national production and often achieve higher per-hectare productivity than estates. The sector faces challenges including labor shortages, aging tea bushes, climate change impacts, and market price volatility. Diversification into value-added products and specialty teas is an ongoing strategic priority.

content: Ceylon tea consistently commands premium prices in global markets due to quality reputation and geographic indication protection. title: Tea Export Markets for Sri Lanka
content: Sri Lankan tea exports reach over 150 countries, with major markets including Russia, Iran, Iraq, Turkey, UAE, and Syria. The Middle East and CIS countries together absorb over 50% of Ceylon tea exports. Japan and China represent growing markets for premium orthodox teas. Western markets including the UK, Germany, and USA value Ceylon tea for blending and increasingly for specialty single-origin products. content: Climate change poses significant threats to tea cultivation in Sri Lanka through altered rainfall patterns, temperature increases, and more frequent extreme weather events. title: Tea Quality Assessment Methods
content: Professional tea quality assessment involves systematic evaluation of dry leaf appearance, infused leaf, and liquor characteristics. Dry leaf is assessed for color uniformity, tip content, particle size consistency, and absence of fiber or foreign matter. The standard tasting protocol uses 2.86 grams of tea infused in 140ml boiling water for exactly 5 minutes. Liquor evaluation covers color, brightness, strength, briskness, body, and quality. Infused leaf assessment reveals processing quality and plucking standard. Professional tasters develop vocabularies including hundreds of descriptive terms. title: Factors Affecting Tea Quality
content: Tea quality results from complex interactions among genetic, environmental, and processing factors. Cultivar determines baseline potential for quality attributes. Elevation profoundly affects quality - higher elevations produce more complex, delicate teas due to slower growth and cooler temperatures. Season influences quality with dry periods generally producing better teas than wet seasons. Plucking standard is critical - fine plucking yields superior tea while coarse plucking produces poor quality regardless of other factors. Soil nutrition affects plant health and leaf composition. Processing skill transforms raw material into finished tea - withering, rolling, oxidation, and drying must each be optimized. Storage conditions preserve or degrade quality over time. title: AI Tea Leaf Quality Grading System
content: The AI-driven tea leaf quality grading system developed for Project 25-26J-133 uses computer vision and machine learning to classify tea shoots into five quality categories. Fresh_Bud_1 (score: 10) represents premium quality with intact bud and 1-2 tender leaves. Fresh_Bud_2 (score: 8) indicates good quality with 2-3 leaves and bud. Coarse_Pluck (score: 0) identifies reject material with 3+ mature leaves. Old_Leaf (score: 0) detects overmature, yellowing leaves. Damaged_Leaf (score: 0) recognizes physical damage, pest holes, or disease symptoms. The classification follows TRI plucking standards and uses a priority-based decision hierarchy: damage is checked first, then age indicators, maturity, and finally freshness. This system aims to provide objective, consistent grading at scale while reducing reliance on human assessment variability.

title: Origins of Ceylon Tea Industry
content: The Ceylon tea industry emerged from the ashes of coffee cultivation following the devastating coffee rust epidemic (Hemileia vastatrix) in the 1860s-1880s that destroyed the island's coffee plantations. Scottish planter James Taylor established the first commercial tea plantation at Loolecondera Estate in Kandy district in 1867, planting seeds from Assam, India. Taylor's experimental plot of 19 acres expanded rapidly as coffee estates converted to tea. By 1872, Taylor had built his first tea factory using Chinese processing methods adapted to local conditions. The first shipment of Ceylon tea reached London in 1873. Thomas Lipton's investment in the 1890s helped popularize Ceylon tea globally. By 1900, tea had completely replaced coffee as Ceylon's primary agricultural export. The industry's rapid development was facilitated by existing plantation infrastructure, labor force, and transportation networks established during the coffee era.

title: Evolution of Ceylon Tea Processing
content: Tea processing in Ceylon evolved from crude manual methods to sophisticated mechanized operations. James Taylor's early techniques adapted Chinese methods with local innovations. The introduction of the Sirocco dryer in 1877 revolutionized drying operations. Rolling machines replaced hand-rolling in the 1880s, enabling larger scale production. British engineer W. Jackson invented the roller specifically for Ceylon conditions. Withering troughs with fan systems replaced natural withering, providing consistent results regardless of weather. The orthodox processing method was standardized during this period, becoming Ceylon's signature approach. While CTC processing was adopted elsewhere in the 20th century, Sri Lanka maintained orthodox focus, preserving traditional quality character. Modern factories combine historical knowledge with contemporary technology including automated fermentation monitoring and computer-controlled drying. This evolution balanced efficiency gains with quality preservation.

title: Colombo Tea Auction
content: The Colombo Tea Auction is one of the world's largest and most important tea trading centers, handling approximately 6 million kilograms weekly. Established in 1883 during the colonial era, the auction operates every Tuesday at the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce. Sellers present samples catalogued by estate, grade, and quality descriptors. Digital innovations are modernizing auction processes while maintaining the fundamental price discovery function. title: Ceylon Tea Trademarks and Certification

content: Page 1 of 2 TEA RESEARCH INSTITUTE OF SRI LANKA Issued In: December 2019 Guideline No: 03/2019 GUIDELINES FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF TEA TO FACILITATE MECHANIZATION OF FIELD OPERATIONS Introduction Tea is a labour-intensive plantation crop; hence, the labour requirement and cost are heavy. It has become necessary to introduce mechanization to tea plantations since the tea sector is presently facing acute worker shortage. Mechanization in agriculture is the use of machine to accomplish a task or operation involved in agricultural production. Key objectives of mechanization are to increase worker productivity, reduc e cost of production, improv e product quality, eas e manual operations, complete tasks timely and change worker attitudes. Tea planting system facilitating mechanization of field operations Mechanization of field operations requires adequate space for worker and machine mobility, dense canopy architecture and absence of obstacles such as shade trees in the path of machine operation. The conventional system of single-row planting at a spacing of 0.6 m x 1.2 m (2 feet X 4 feet) limits the use and efficiency of machines. The double hedge -row planting system commonly practiced in some other tea growing countries such as Japan and China paves the way for mechanizing most of the labour - intensive field operations such as harvesting successfully. Therefore, hedge -row planting system having a spacing of 0.6 m x 0.6 m x 1.5 m (2 feet X 2 feet X 5 feet: Figure 1) is considered amenable to facilitate mechanization of post -planting tea field operations in Sri Lanka. However, the other special considerations that require greater attention are as follows;  As considerable space of land between two hedge-rows is exposed to rain thus soil erosion, this planting system is more suitable for flat and undulating lands. The Integrated Weed Management (IWM) approach includes preventive, manual, biological, cultural, mechanical and chemical methods (in rotation) as defined by the most current TRI circular on Weed Management. Tea gardens must limit chemical weeding to levels of inputs and application frequency as defined by the up-to-date version of the TRI advisory circular on Chemical control of weeds in tea lands. 4.2/ Plucking 0. The tea bushes are plucked at required intervals of 6 to 10 days to ensure a regular renewal of juvenile leaves and a bud. 1. Plucking can be done by hand or by a mechanical device. A sub-labelling of “Hand plucked” can be used for tea that is 100% hand plucked. 2. Plucking standard is systematically determined at factory gate according to the three categories of plucking standards defined in the “quality of the raw material” (part 3.2) 4.3/ Transport of green leaf 0. The green leaves must be transported in a way to preserve the quality of the leaves from farm gate (or collection point) to factory. 1. Green leaves must be delivered to the factory before 8:30PM on the same day they have been plucked. 2. Green leaf transport must be done with one or more approved containers recommended by the Tea Commissioner if located from and more than 5 km from the factory: 1. Plastic crates with a maximum load of 20 kg. 17 2. Coir sacks (80cm x 65cm - minimum size) with a maximum load of 18 kg. 3. Nylon sacks (90cm x 70cm) with a maximum load of 20 kg. 4. Transport vehicles must be adapted and equipped for the transport of fresh green tea leaves. Collection lorries must be ventilated and equipped with racks and/or shelves for sacks handling. There should also be protection against the rain.

By the end of the century, the emerging tea industry soon surpassed all successes of its coffee predecessor in terms of export volumes, revenues and area under cultivation3. 6.2/ Historical reputation of ‘Ceylon tea’ 6.2.1/ ‘Ceylon tea’ name Under British rule, from 1815 to 1948, Sri Lanka was known as Ceylon, a name it kept for nearly a quarter-century after independence. The English name Ceylon is derived from Sihala, which is a poor rendering of the Sinhalese name of the island. The Arabic name(s) – Serendip, Serendiv, Singaldip - is derived from Sinhaladvipa. Similarly, the Greek name – Sheelan, Sielen Diva and ‘Salike’ also derived from the name Sinhala - the land of the Sinhalas. From the name Sielen, many European forms were derived: the Portuguese Ceilão, Spanish Ceilán, Dutch Zeilan, Ceilan, Seylon; French Selon, Ceylan and the Latin Zeylan. Ceylon gained independence on the 4 February 1948. In 1972, a new constitution was enacted, and Ceylon became the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka. However, the name ‘Ceylon’ remained for the most famous national ‘brands’, such as tea or cinnamon. Indeed, the name ‘Ceylon tea’ has been used in trade since the 1880s4. At present, the Sri Lanka tea industry involves more than 397,233 smallholdings (2005) and 328 tea estates (293 in RPCs & 35 in States) (MAPI, 2018); 1,596 registered tea leaf dealers; 782 active registered factories; 8 registered tea brokers; 386 registered tea exporters and 189 registered packers (Sri Lanka Tea Board (SLTB, 2022)). 1 History of Ceylon Tea | Sri Lanka Tea Board. https://www.srilankateaboard.lk/ceylon-tea/history-of-ceylon-tea/. Located on a tropical island (between 5° 55' to 9° 51' North latitude and between 79° 42' to 81° 53' East longitude) ‘Ceylon tea’ cultivation extends over an altitude gradient ranging from sea level up to high altitudes (above 1200 meters). In the tea sector, it is therefore common to refer first to ‘Ceylon tea’ growing area by their altitude, namely: the “low country” (ranging from sea level to 600m), “mid country” (600m to 1200m) and “up country” (above 1200m). The agro-climatic specificities of ‘Ceylon tea’ are defined by an important diversity in climate in the tea growing areas. This is a signification feature in the wet and intermediate zones of Sri Lanka. The rainfall pattern is distinctly seasonal with two pics. More specifically, rainfalls are paced by the South-West monsoon from May to September, and the North-East monsoon from December to February, followed by inter-monsoonal rains covering the whole island (March-April and October-November). The central mountains act as a divider between those two annual climatic events, which results in different periods of rainfall on either side of the mountains. The amount of rainfall and its distributions are the most important factors that affect the productivity of tea. The number of rainless days in the wet zone is very small compared to the total number of rainy days in a year. In addition, the agro-climatic conditions of the delimited geographical area offer good exposition to solar radiation. The mean annual sunshine duration in the wet zone ranges from 4.9 to 6.4 hours per day depending on the location. Colombo Auction – The auction system can be considered as part of the cultural heritage that showcases the ‘Ceylon tea’ quality and contributes to its truthful recognition. Tea auctions were first introduced in Colombo in 1883, on the premises of Somerville & Co., a Colombo merchant house, on the basis of those conducted at Mincing Lane in London. By the turn of the century, most of the estates were owned by joint-stock companies, either listed in sterling or in rupee. Shareholders of those companies were British, often far from the plantations. The management in the estates was delegated to ‘management companies’ or ‘agency houses’, which handled the cultivation, processing and sale of tea. In Colombo, the agency houses employed teams of expert tea-tasters to sample and report on the quality of each estate’s produce before it was put up for auction in Colombo or London. The brokers and buyers, too, had their tasters, and it was tasters from both sides who attended the auctions. Once established, the structure of the ‘tea trade’ was little altered. Overseen by trade associations such as the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce (est. 1839) and the Colombo Tea Traders’ Association (est. 1894), it continued to function with little change in operational procedure, management style or ownership structure throughout the colonial period and was British-dominated23. The Colombo tea auction in Sri Lanka now operates as an online platform; the first historical online auction was successfully conducted on 4 April 2020.
